narrative:
The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average student who was accepted ranked around the 5.8th decile in their third year, you placed in the 2nd decile. This lower standing was the main reason the model saw higher risk.

Your LSAT score of 38 worked in the opposite direction. It is slightly above the average of accepted students (37.2), so it helped pull the prediction toward passing, though not enough to overcome the other factors. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.4 similarly provided a modest positive push, as it sits above the 3.23 average of accepted applicants.

In short, while your test scores and college grades were solid, your much weaker performance in the third year of law school was the dominant signal that led to the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your third-year performance and consider retaking the bar exam preparation courses that target the specific areas where your class rank slipped. Improving that record in a visible way will have the biggest impact on future applications. (218 words)
